86121.m: Empty space is about minus 270 degrees.

86122.q: What is the coldest temperature there can possibly be called?
86122.e: Absolute zero is minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. Nothing can be colder.
86122.m: Nothing can get colder than absolute zero.

86123.q: How hot can it get on the Moon during the day?
86123.e: When the Sun shines on the Moon, the ground gets hotter than 100 degrees.
86123.m: During the day the Moon's surface gets scorching hot.

86124.q: How cold can it get on the Moon at night?
86124.e: During the lunar night the ground cools down a lot. It gets far colder than minus 100 degrees.
86124.m: The lunar night is bitterly cold.

86125.q: Why does it get so hot and so cold on the Moon?
a: It has no air to even out the heat
It is made entirely of ice
It is very close to the Sun
86125.e: On Earth the air acts like a blanket. The Moon has no such atmosphere, so the temperature changes a lot.
86125.m: Without air there is no protective blanket against heat and cold.

86126.q: What is it like far out near the planet Neptune?
86126.e: Neptune is very far from the Sun. Only a little warmth gets there, so it is freezing cold.
86126.m: The further from the Sun, the colder it gets.

86127.q: What happens to an object in space when the Sun shines directly on it?
86127.e: In sunlight it gets very hot in space, in the shade very cold. So spacecraft need good protection.
86127.m: In space it is hot in the sun and icy cold in the shade.

86128.q: Why does the James Webb Space Telescope have a huge sunshield?
a: So it does not get wet
86128.e: The telescope has to be very cold to work well. The shield keeps out the Sun's heat.
86128.m: The sunshield keeps the James Webb Telescope cold.

86129.q: In what form is water found on the Moon?
86129.e: The Sun never shines into deep, dark craters at the Moon's poles. It is always icy cold there, and there is water ice.
86129.m: There is water ice in dark craters on the Moon.

86130.q: How loud is it in empty space?
a: There is a constant rushing noise
86130.e: There is no air in empty space. So you cannot hear anything there.
86130.m: In space there is complete silence.

86131.q: How do astronauts talk to each other during a spacewalk?
86131.e: Out in space there is no air to carry the voice. So the astronauts have radios in their helmets.
86131.m: In space astronauts talk by radio.

86132.q: Could you hear an explosion in space?
a: Yes, but only during the day
86132.e: Without air, the bang cannot spread. You could only see the explosion, not hear it.
86132.m: In space every bang is silent.

86133.q: Is it completely silent on the ISS space station?
a: Yes, you hear nothing at all
Yes, because it is in space
No, only because of the rockets
86133.e: On the ISS there is air to breathe. That is why you can hear noises there, for example from fans and pumps.
86133.m: On the space station there is air and so there are also noises.

86134.q: What does sound need to travel?
86134.e: Sound is made when air or another material vibrates back and forth. Without a material there is no sound.
86134.m: Sound needs air, water or another material.

86135.q: Can light travel through empty space?
a: Yes, light does not need air
86135.e: Unlike sound, light does not need air. That is why we can see the stars but not hear them.
86135.m: Light gets through empty space too.

86136.q: How do space probes send messages through silent space to Earth?
86136.e: Radio waves are a kind of invisible light. They reach the Earth even without air.
86136.m: Space probes radio their data to Earth.

86137.q: What cannot escape from a black hole?
86137.e: A black hole pulls so strongly that even light cannot get out. That is why it looks black.
86137.m: Not even light gets out of a black hole.

86138.q: How does a black hole often form?
a: A giant star collapses in on itself
86138.e: When a very large star collapses at the end of its life, a black hole can form.
86138.m: Black holes often form from giant stars.

86139.q: Where is there a giant black hole?
a: In the middle of the Milky Way
86139.e: At the centre of our galaxy, the Milky Way, there is a giant black hole. It is very far away from us.
86139.m: There is a giant black hole in the middle of the Milky Way.

86140.q: In which year was the first picture of a black hole shown?
86140.e: In 2019 researchers showed the first picture. You can see a bright ring around a dark spot.
86140.m: The first picture of a black hole has existed since 2019.

86141.q: Could a black hole swallow the Earth soon?
a: No, all known ones are very far away
Yes, as soon as next year
Yes, one is already very close
86141.e: All known black holes are unimaginably far from the Earth. We are not in danger.
86141.m: No black hole is dangerously close to the Earth.

86142.q: Why does a black hole pull everything so strongly?
86142.e: In a black hole a great deal of mass is packed into a tiny space. This creates enormous gravity.
86142.m: A black hole has enormous gravity.

86143.q: How do researchers recognise a black hole, even though it cannot be seen directly?
a: By stars and gas circling it
86143.e: Stars and gas move very fast around the black hole. That is how researchers notice that it is there.
86143.m: You recognise a black hole by what circles it.

86144.q: What is the boundary around a black hole called, beyond which nothing comes back?
86144.e: Whatever crosses the event horizon never comes out again. It is like an invisible boundary.
86144.m: Beyond the event horizon there is no way back.

86145.q: Have researchers found life outside the Earth yet (as of 2025)?
86145.e: By 2025, life had not been found anywhere else. The Earth is the only place where we know for certain that there is life.
86145.m: So far we only know of life on Earth.

86146.q: What is especially important for life as we know it?
86146.e: All living things on Earth need liquid water. That is why researchers look for water in space.
86146.m: Without liquid water there is no life as we know it.

86147.q: On which planet are robot vehicles searching for traces of past life?
86147.e: Mars once had rivers and lakes. Rovers such as Perseverance are searching there for traces of life.
86147.m: Rovers are searching for traces of life on Mars.

86148.q: What are planets that orbit stars other than the Sun called?
86148.e: Exoplanets lie outside our solar system. Thousands of them are already known today.
86148.m: Planets around other stars are called exoplanets.

86149.q: Which two Swiss researchers found the first planet around a Sun-like star in 1995?
86149.e: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz from the University of Geneva discovered this planet. They received the Nobel Prize for it in 2019.
86149.m: Two Geneva researchers found the first planet around a Sun-like star.

86150.q: Which of Jupiter's moons probably has a large ocean under its ice?
86150.e: Researchers think there is an ocean of salt water under the thick layer of ice on Jupiter's moon Europa.
86150.m: There is probably an ocean under the ice of the moon Europa.

86151.q: What instruments do researchers use to listen for radio signals from aliens?
86151.e: Radio telescopes are large aerials. Researchers use them to search the sky for signals that are not natural.
86151.m: Radio telescopes listen out into space.

86152.q: What do the Voyager space probes carry as a greeting to aliens?
86152.e: Greetings, music and sounds from the Earth are stored on the golden record.
86152.m: The Voyager probes carry a golden record with greetings.

86153.q: Which of Saturn's moons sprays fountains of water into space?
86153.e: Fountains of water shoot out of cracks in the ice of Enceladus. There is probably an ocean underneath.
86153.m: Saturn's moon Enceladus sprays water into space.

86154.q: How heavy do you feel on the Moon compared with the Earth?
86154.e: The Moon pulls only about a sixth as strongly as the Earth. That is why you feel much lighter there.
86154.m: On the Moon you weigh only about a sixth.

86155.q: A child weighs 30 kg on Earth. Roughly what would a set of scales show on the Moon?
86155.e: On the Moon you weigh about a sixth. 30 divided by 6 is 5.
86155.m: On the Moon the scales show only a sixth.

86156.q: Why are you lighter on the Moon than on the Earth?
a: There is no air on the Moon
86156.e: The Moon is much smaller and lighter than the Earth. That is why it pulls more weakly.
86156.m: A small body in space pulls less strongly.

86157.q: How did the astronauts often move forwards on the Moon?
86157.e: Because you are so light on the Moon, small jumps were a good way to get along.
86157.m: On the Moon the astronauts hopped like kangaroos.

86158.q: Roughly how high could you jump on the Moon compared with the Earth?
86158.e: The Moon pulls about six times more weakly. So in a jump you fly about six times as high.
86158.m: On the Moon you jump about six times as high.

86159.q: Do you get thinner on the Moon because you weigh less?
a: No, your body stays the same
86159.e: Your body does not change. Only the pull is weaker, so the scales show less.
86159.m: On the Moon you are lighter, but not thinner.

86160.q: How does a ball fall to the ground on the Moon compared with the Earth?
86160.e: Because the Moon pulls more weakly, the ball falls more gently. But it still comes back down.
86160.m: On the Moon things fall to the ground more slowly.

86161.q: Why does a ripe apple fall down from the tree?
86161.e: The Earth pulls all things towards it. This force is called gravity.

86162.q: Which famous scientist explained gravity, supposedly after seeing a falling apple?
86162.e: Isaac Newton lived in England over 300 years ago. He explained why things fall and planets orbit.

86163.q: What keeps the Moon in its orbit around the Earth?
86163.e: The Earth pulls the Moon. That is why it does not fly away but circles us.
86163.m: The Earth's gravity holds on to the Moon.

86164.q: An astronaut on the Moon dropped a hammer and a feather at the same time. What happened?
a: Both landed at the same time
86164.e: On the Moon there is no air to slow the feather down. That is why the hammer and the feather fall equally fast.
86164.m: Without air, all things fall equally fast.

86165.q: On which planet would you be much heavier than on Earth?
86165.e: Jupiter is huge and pulls strongly. There you would be about two and a half times as heavy as on Earth.
86165.m: On Jupiter you would be much heavier.

86166.q: Roughly how much do you weigh on Mars compared with the Earth?
86166.e: Mars is smaller than the Earth and pulls more weakly. You weigh only just over a third there.
86166.m: On Mars you weigh just over a third.

86167.q: What holds the air around the Earth in place?
86167.e: Gravity holds the atmosphere in place. Without it, the air would escape into space.
86167.m: Gravity keeps our air at the Earth.

86168.q: In a model, the Sun is as big as a football. How big is the Earth then?
86168.e: The Sun is about 109 times wider than the Earth. With a football of 22 cm, the Earth is only about 2 mm across.
86168.m: Next to a football Sun, the Earth is tiny.

86169.q: In a model, the Sun is a football of 22 cm. How far away is the Earth then?
86169.e: The distance from the Earth to the Sun is about 108 times the width of the Sun. 22 cm times 108 makes about 24 metres.
86169.m: In a model the planets are far apart.

86170.q: Why would a model of the solar system to the correct scale hardly fit in a classroom?
86170.e: The planets are small, but the distances are huge. A proper model would be many kilometres long.
86170.m: The solar system is mostly empty space.

86171.q: What is a model called that shows how the Earth and the Moon circle the Sun?
86171.e: A tellurion has a lamp or a ball as the Sun. You turn a handle to move the Earth and the Moon around it.
86171.m: A tellurion shows the Sun, the Earth and the Moon in motion.

86172.q: What is the domed hall at the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne called, where the night sky is projected onto the ceiling?
86172.e: In a planetarium you see stars and planets on a round ceiling. The Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne has one.
86172.m: In a planetarium the night sky shines on the ceiling.

86173.q: In a model, everything is a billion times smaller. How big is the Sun then?
86173.e: The Sun is about 1.4 million km across. A billion times smaller, that is about 1.4 metres.
86173.m: Even greatly scaled down, the Sun is still big.

86174.q: What did many people in the past think was at the centre of the universe?
86174.e: In the past, people believed that the Sun and the stars went round the Earth. This is called the geocentric view of the world.
86174.m: People once believed the Earth was the centre of the universe.

86175.q: Who wrote around 500 years ago that the Earth goes round the Sun?
86175.e: Nicolaus Copernicus put the Sun in the middle. His book came out in 1543.
86175.m: Copernicus put the Sun at the centre of the solar system.

86176.q: What happens during a lunar eclipse?
a: The Moon passes through the Earth's shadow
86176.e: During a lunar eclipse the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. Its shadow falls on the Moon.
86176.m: During a lunar eclipse the Moon is in the Earth's shadow.

86177.q: Who can see a lunar eclipse?
a: Everyone who has the Moon in their sky at the time
Only people at the North Pole
86177.e: The Moon is then in the Earth's shadow. That is why you can see the eclipse everywhere on the night side of the Earth where the Moon is visible.
86177.m: A lunar eclipse can be seen on the whole night side of the Earth.

86178.q: Why does the Moon glow reddish during a total lunar eclipse?
a: The Earth's atmosphere bends red light towards it
The Moon gets hot and glows
A fire is burning on the Moon
86178.e: The Earth's air bends some sunlight into the shadow. Mainly red light reaches the Moon this way.
86178.m: Red light from the Earth's air colours the eclipsed Moon.

86179.q: What is the Moon often called during a total lunar eclipse because of its colour?
86179.e: Because the Moon then looks dark red, many people call it a blood moon.
86179.m: The red Moon during an eclipse is called a blood moon.

86180.q: In what order are the Sun, the Earth and the Moon during a lunar eclipse?
86180.e: The Earth is in the middle. That way its shadow falls exactly on the Moon.
86180.m: During a lunar eclipse the Earth is in the middle.

86181.q: What shape is the Earth's shadow that falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse?
86181.e: The edge of the shadow on the Moon is curved. Over 2000 years ago, people concluded from this that the Earth is a sphere.
86181.m: The Earth's round shadow shows that the Earth is a sphere.

86182.q: Where can you see the Earth's shadow as a dark blue band in the sky after sunset?
a: On the side opposite the Sun
86182.e: The Earth casts its shadow into the air. You can see it low in the sky on the opposite side from the Sun.
86182.m: In the evening the Earth's shadow rises in the east.

86183.q: What is the pink band called that glows above the Earth's shadow at twilight?
86183.e: A pink band often glows above the dark shadow of the Earth. It is called the Belt of Venus.
86183.m: The pink band above the Earth's shadow is called the Belt of Venus.

86184.q: Is it all right to look at a lunar eclipse without protective glasses?
86184.e: The Moon does not shine as harshly as the Sun. You can watch a lunar eclipse without protection.
86184.m: You can watch a lunar eclipse without protective glasses.

86185.q: Which sea is closest to Switzerland?
86185.e: From Ticino to the coast near Genoa in Italy it is only about 150 km. Switzerland itself has no coastline.
86185.m: The Mediterranean is the nearest sea to Switzerland.

86186.q: Which ocean lies around the North Pole?
86186.e: The Arctic Ocean lies around the North Pole. It is the smallest ocean and is often covered with ice.
86186.m: The Arctic Ocean is at the North Pole.

86187.q: Which ocean lies between Africa and Australia?
86187.e: The Indian Ocean lies south of India. It stretches from Africa to Australia.
86187.m: The Indian Ocean lies between Africa and Australia.

86188.q: What does the name Pacific mean?
86188.e: The explorer Magellan had calm weather there. So he called it the peaceful ocean.

86189.q: What makes most of the waves on the sea?
86189.e: The wind blows over the water and pushes it up into waves.
86189.m: The wind makes the waves on the sea.

86190.q: What is a huge wave caused by an undersea earthquake called?
86190.e: An earthquake on the seabed can lift the water strongly. This creates a tsunami, which causes great damage on the coast.
86190.m: An undersea earthquake can cause a tsunami.

86191.q: What is the highest point of a wave called?
86191.e: The crest is the top of the wave. That is where the water is highest.
86191.m: The top of a wave is the crest.

86192.q: What does a ball in the sea do when a wave passes under it?
a: It rises and falls in almost the same place
It flies far along with the wave
It spins in a circle around a ship
86192.e: In a wave, it is mainly the movement that travels on. The water itself moves almost only up and down.
86192.m: A wave carries the movement on, not the water.

86193.q: Which sport do you do on ocean waves with a board?
86193.e: When surfing, you glide down the wave on a board. You need good waves for it.
86193.m: You can surf on the waves.

86194.q: What is the lowest point between two waves called?
86194.e: Between two wave crests there is a dip. This is called a trough.
86194.m: Between two waves is the trough.

86195.q: What happens to the waves when the wind blows harder?
86195.e: The stronger and longer the wind blows, the more energy it gives the water. The waves get higher.

86196.q: What do you call a single, especially high wave in the middle of the ocean?
86196.e: Rogue waves are much higher than the waves around them. They are rare but dangerous for ships.
86196.m: A rogue wave is a sudden giant wave on the open sea.

86197.q: What does a line of washed-up seaweed and shells on the beach show?
a: How high the water came at high tide
Where you are allowed to swim
86197.e: At high tide, the sea washes up seaweed, shells and wood. When the water goes back, a line is left behind.
86197.m: The strandline shows how far the tide came.

86198.q: Why do some beaches, for example in Iceland, have black sand?
a: The sand comes from volcanic rock
86198.e: The sea grinds dark volcanic rock into sand. This makes black sand.
86198.m: Black sand comes from volcanic rock.

86199.q: What is the white sand on many beaches in the Caribbean made of?
86199.e: In warm seas, coral and seashells are ground into fine, light sand.
86199.m: White Caribbean sand often comes from coral and shells.

86200.q: Which sea animals lay their eggs in the sand on the beach?
86200.e: Sea turtles crawl ashore at night and bury their eggs in the sand. The young hatch later on their own.
86200.m: Sea turtles lay their eggs on the beach.

86201.q: Why does a sandcastle made of wet sand hold better than one made of dry sand?
a: The water holds the grains together
Wet sand is made of clay
86201.e: Tiny water bridges form between the grains. They hold the grains together like glue.
86201.m: Wet sand sticks, dry sand trickles.

86202.q: Which animal often walks sideways across the sand on the beach?
86202.e: Crabs have legs that work best for walking sideways. That way they quickly disappear into holes.

86203.q: What does a red flag mean on many beaches?
86203.e: A red flag warns of danger, such as high waves or a strong current. Then you must not go into the water.
86203.m: When the red flag is up, stay out of the water.

86204.q: What do you call a beach with lots of small stones instead of sand?
86204.e: Pebble beaches are made of small, round stones. You often find them on the Mediterranean and on Swiss lakes.
86204.m: A beach of small stones is a pebble beach.

86205.q: What is a hill of sand piled up by the wind called?
86205.e: The wind carries grains of sand and drops them where it gets weaker. That is how a dune grows.
86205.m: A dune is a sand hill built by the wind.

86206.q: Which side of a dune is usually steeper?
a: The side facing away from the wind
The side the wind comes from
Both sides are always equally steep
86206.e: The wind pushes the sand up the gentle side. Behind the ridge, the sand slides down and forms a steep slope.
86206.m: A dune is steep on the side away from the wind.

a: Yes, the wind pushes them along
No, they always stay in place
86207.e: The wind blows sand over the dune. So it slowly moves on. It is then called a moving dune.
86207.m: Moving dunes slowly travel with the wind.

86208.q: Which plant holds the sand of the dunes in place on the North Sea?
86208.e: Marram grass has very long roots. With them it holds the sand so the wind cannot carry it away.
86208.m: Marram grass holds dunes in place.

86209.q: In which country is the Dune of Pilat, the highest moving dune in Europe?
86209.e: The Dune of Pilat lies on the Atlantic coast of France. It is about 100 metres high.
86209.m: Europe’s highest dune is in France.

86210.q: Why should you not walk all over the dunes on the coast?
a: Otherwise the plants that hold the sand get damaged
Because the sand is too hot
86210.e: If the plants are trampled, the wind can blow the dune away. Dunes protect the land from the sea.
86210.m: Staying on the paths protects the dunes.

86211.q: What is a dune shaped like a half-moon called?
86211.e: A crescent dune has two tips pointing with the wind. It looks like a crescent moon.
86211.m: A crescent dune is shaped like a half-moon.

86212.q: What can some dunes do when sand slides down them?
86212.e: When a lot of sand slides, the grains rub against each other. This makes a deep humming sound. People speak of singing dunes.
86212.m: There are dunes that can hum.

86213.q: In which large desert in Africa are there huge sand dunes?
86213.e: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world. In some parts there are huge fields of dunes.
86213.m: There are huge dunes in the Sahara.

86214.q: What is the largest island in Lake Zurich called?
86214.e: Ufenau lies in Lake Zurich and belongs to the canton of Schwyz. You reach it by boat, because there is no bridge.
86214.m: Ufenau is an island in Lake Zurich.

86215.q: What do you call a group of many islands close together?
86215.e: An archipelago is a group of islands. One example is the many islands of Greece.
86215.m: Many islands together form an archipelago.

86216.q: What is a ring-shaped island made of coral called?
86216.e: An atoll is a ring of coral. In its middle there is an area of water.
86216.m: An atoll is a ring-shaped coral island.

86217.q: Which country in northern Europe is a large volcanic island in the Atlantic?
86217.e: Iceland lies in the North Atlantic and has many volcanoes and hot springs.
86217.m: Iceland is a volcanic island in the north.

86218.q: On which islands in the Pacific do famous giant tortoises live?
86218.e: Giant tortoises that can live for more than 100 years live on the Galápagos Islands.
86218.m: Giant tortoises live on the Galápagos Islands.

86219.e: When waves hit the coast, they break and foam. This is called surf.
86219.m: Surf forms when waves break on the coast.

86220.q: Why do waves break near the shore?
86220.e: In shallow water, the bottom of the wave is slowed down. The top is faster, tips forward and breaks.
86220.m: In shallow water, waves tip over and break.

86221.q: Why does the foam of the surf look white?
a: Because it contains lots of tiny air bubbles
Because there is soap in the sea
86221.e: When the wave breaks, a lot of air is mixed into the water. The many bubbles make the foam look white.
86221.m: Air bubbles make the foam white.

86222.q: What are the fine drops of water that splash into the air from the surf called?
86222.e: When waves crash against rocks, fine drops splash up. This is called spray.
86222.m: Water splashed up by the surf is called spray.

86223.q: What is a dangerous current that pulls water from the beach back out to sea called?
86223.e: The water of the surf flows back out to sea quickly in narrow channels. This rip current can pull swimmers out.
86223.m: A rip current pulls away from the beach out to sea.

86224.q: What should you do if a current pulls you away from the beach?
a: Swim sideways, parallel to the beach
Swim against the current with all your strength
86224.e: The current is usually only narrow. If you swim out sideways, you get out of it and can then get back to the shore.
86224.m: In a current, swim sideways along the beach.

86225.q: What does the surf do to sharp-edged stones over a long time?
86225.e: The waves roll the stones back and forth again and again. This grinds off the edges.

86226.q: When is the surf especially wild?
86226.e: A storm makes high waves. When they crash against the coast, the surf roars especially loudly.
86226.m: In a storm, the surf roars.

86228.q: Near which town in England are there famous white chalk cliffs?
86228.e: The White Cliffs of Dover are made of chalk. You can see them from a ship from far away.
86228.m: White chalk cliffs shine at Dover.

86229.q: On which German island in the Baltic Sea are there white chalk cliffs?
86229.e: On the island of Rügen, pale chalk cliffs rise steeply above the Baltic Sea. They are very well known.
86229.m: Rügen is famous for its chalk cliffs.

a: The waves wear away the rock until it breaks off
86230.e: The waves hollow out the rock at the bottom. At some point the upper part breaks off, and a steep wall forms.
86230.m: The waves eat into the rock and shape cliffs.

86231.q: Which seabird with a colourful beak nests on cliffs in the north?
86231.e: Puffins have an orange-striped beak. They nest in burrows on steep coasts, for example in Iceland.
86231.m: The puffin nests on steep coasts.

86232.q: What is a rock arch that the sea has washed out of a cliff called?
86232.e: The waves wash a hole through a rocky headland. What is left is an arch that the sea flows through.
86232.m: The sea can wash arches into the rocks.

86233.q: What is a single pillar of rock standing in the sea in front of a cliff called?
86233.e: When a sea arch collapses, a single pillar is often left standing in the sea.
86233.m: A sea stack stands alone in front of the coast.

86234.q: Why should you not go right to the edge of a cliff?
86234.e: The sea hollows out the rocks from below. So the edge can suddenly break off.
86234.m: Keep your distance from the edge of a cliff.

86235.e: A lot of salt is dissolved in seawater. Streams, rain and mountain lakes, on the other hand, have fresh water.

86236.q: Can you drink seawater when you are thirsty?
a: No, it makes you even thirstier
Yes, as much as you like
86236.e: All the salt draws water out of the body. Anyone who drinks seawater gets even thirstier.

86237.q: In which lake is the water so salty that you almost float on top by yourself?
86237.e: The Dead Sea is much saltier than the ocean. The heavy salt water carries your body like an air mattress.
86237.m: In the Dead Sea you hardly sink.

86238.q: Why is it easier to float in the sea than in a Swiss lake?
a: There are waves in the sea
The water in the lake is deeper
86238.e: Salt water is heavier than fresh water. So it pushes the body upwards more strongly.
86238.m: Salt water carries you better than fresh water.

a: Seawater is left to evaporate in the sun
It is dug up on the beach
It is collected from the seabed
86239.e: In shallow pools, the water evaporates in the sun. The salt is left over and is raked together.
86239.m: Sea salt is left over when seawater evaporates.

86240.q: The salt in Switzerland comes from the ground. How did it form long ago?
a: From an ancient sea that dried up
86240.e: More than 200 million years ago there was a sea here. When it dried up, the salt was left behind and later covered over.
86240.m: Swiss salt comes from an ancient sea.

86241.q: What do you call water with very little salt, like in lakes and rivers?
86241.e: The water in streams, rivers and most lakes contains hardly any salt. It is called fresh water.
86241.m: Lakes and rivers have fresh water.

86242.q: Where is the deepest point of all the oceans?
86242.e: The Mariana Trench is in the Pacific. The seabed there is deeper than anywhere else.
86242.m: The deepest point of the oceans is in the Mariana Trench.

86243.q: Roughly how deep is the deepest point in the ocean?
86243.e: The deepest point is almost 11,000 metres below sea level. Mount Everest would fit inside it.
86243.m: The deepest point of the ocean is about 11,000 metres deep.

86244.q: What is it like on the seabed of the deep sea?
86244.e: Sunlight only reaches a few hundred metres down into the water. Below that it is completely dark.
86244.m: The deep sea is pitch dark.

86245.q: What is there on the seabed?
86245.e: The seabed is very varied. There are huge mountain ranges, deep trenches and volcanoes.
86245.m: There are mountains and valleys under the sea too.

86246.q: Which Swiss man was one of the first people to dive into the Mariana Trench in 1960?
86246.e: In 1960, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh dived in the submersible Trieste to the bottom of the Mariana Trench.
86246.m: Jacques Piccard dived to the deepest point of the ocean in 1960.

86247.q: Which deep-sea fish lures prey with a glowing bait?
86247.e: The anglerfish has a kind of fishing rod with a light on its head. Small animals swim towards the light and get eaten.
86247.m: The anglerfish catches prey with light.

86248.q: What do corals build on the seabed in warm seas?
86248.e: Corals are small animals with a limestone skeleton. Together they build large reefs over a long time.

86249.q: What is it like right at the bottom of the seabed?
86249.e: Sunlight only gets a little way into the water. Right at the bottom of the seabed it is pitch dark.
86249.m: Deep down in the sea it is dark.

86250.q: Why does a submersible for the deep sea need very thick walls?
a: The water presses very hard down there
There are rocks in the water there
86250.e: The deeper you dive, the more water presses down from above. In the deep sea this pressure is enormous.
86250.m: In the depths the water presses very hard.

86251.q: What is a shallow body of water on the coast that is almost cut off from the sea called?
86251.e: A lagoon is a shallow basin of seawater. It is connected to the sea only by narrow openings.
86251.m: A lagoon is almost cut off from the sea.

86252.q: Which famous city in Italy was built in a lagoon?
86252.e: Venice stands on many small islands in a lagoon. Instead of streets there are many canals.

86253.q: Which boat is typical of the canals in Venice?
86253.e: The black gondola is steered by a gondolier with an oar. It belongs to Venice.
86253.m: The gondola is the typical boat of Venice.

86254.q: What colour is the water in a South Sea lagoon often?
86254.e: The water in the lagoon is shallow and clear. Over the pale sand it shines turquoise blue.
86254.m: South Sea lagoons shine turquoise blue.

86255.q: Why is the water in a lagoon often warmer than in the open sea?
a: Because it is shallow and the sun warms it
Because there are hot springs in it
86255.e: Shallow water is warmed up quickly by the sun. That is why a lagoon is often pleasantly warm.

86256.q: In which country is the famous “Blue Lagoon”, a warm pool of thermal water?
86256.e: The Blue Lagoon in Iceland is fed by warm water from deep underground. It shines a milky blue.
86256.m: The Blue Lagoon is in Iceland.

86257.q: Which pink birds are often seen in lagoons by the Mediterranean?
86257.e: Flamingos stand in shallow water and eat small shrimps. That is where they get their pink colour.
86257.m: Flamingos like living in shallow lagoons.

86258.q: What often separates a lagoon from the open sea?
86258.e: Waves and currents deposit sand. This creates a narrow strip that shields the lagoon.
86258.m: A strip of sand protects the lagoon from the sea.

86259.q: Which country is especially famous for its fjords?
86259.e: The coast of Norway has more than a thousand fjords. Many people travel there to see them.
86259.m: Norway is the land of fjords.

86260.q: What carved out the deep valleys of the fjords long ago?
86260.e: In the Ice Age, huge glaciers scraped out deep valleys. Later the sea flowed in.

86261.q: What is the longest fjord in Norway called?
86261.e: The Sognefjord is about 200 km long. It reaches far inland.
86261.m: The Sognefjord is Norway’s longest fjord.

86262.q: In which country are there especially many fjords?
86262.e: Norway’s coast is cut by many fjords. The Geirangerfjord is even a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
86262.m: Norway is the land of fjords.

86263.q: Which other country also has many fjords?
86263.e: In the south of New Zealand, glaciers also shaped fjords. There they are often called “sounds”.

86264.q: What kind of water is in a fjord?
86264.e: A fjord is an arm of the sea. So it contains salt water, often mixed at the top with some fresh water from rivers.

a: No, a fjord is connected to the sea
Yes, it is the longest fjord
86265.e: Lake Lucerne is a freshwater lake. A real fjord is an arm of the sea.
86265.m: A fjord always belongs to the sea.

a: A mound of sand in shallow water
A wooden bench on the beach
86266.e: A sandbank is a deposit of sand in the sea or a river. It lies just below or above the water.
86266.m: A sandbank lies in shallow water.

86267.q: Why are sandbanks dangerous for ships?
a: Ships can run aground on them
86267.e: Because the water over a sandbank is shallow, a ship can get stuck. This is called running aground.
86267.m: Ships have to steer around sandbanks.

86268.q: When do many sandbanks in the North Sea appear above the water?
86268.e: At low tide, the sea draws back. Then many sandbanks come to the surface.

86269.q: Which animals like to rest on sandbanks in the North Sea?
86269.e: Seals lie on sandbanks in the sun and rest. At high tide they go back into the water.

86270.q: What shows ships where a sandbank is?
86270.e: Floating buoys mark dangerous places in the water. That way captains know where they can sail.

86271.q: Does a sandbank always stay in the same place?
a: Yes, it is glued to the bottom
No, it floats like a boat
86271.e: Currents and waves carry sand away and deposit it elsewhere. So sandbanks slowly move.

86272.q: How deep is the water over a sandbank?
a: As deep as a house is tall
86272.e: A sandbank is a hill of sand under water. So the water over it is very shallow.
86272.m: The water over a sandbank is shallow.

86273.q: Which gas makes party balloons float upwards?
86273.e: Helium is much lighter than air. That is why a balloon filled with helium floats upwards.
86273.m: A helium balloon rises because helium is lighter than air.

86274.q: What happens to a helium balloon after a few days?
86274.e: The helium slowly escapes through the skin of the balloon. That is why the balloon gets smaller and sinks to the ground.
86274.m: A helium balloon loses its gas over time.

86275.e: Helium is a noble gas and does not burn. That is why it is safe for balloons.
86275.m: Helium does not burn, so it is safe.

86276.q: Which object in the sky is helium named after?
86276.e: Helium was first discovered in the light of the Sun. ‘Helios’ is the Greek word for sun.
86276.m: Helium gets its name from the Sun.

86277.e: Helium is an invisible gas. You cannot see it.

86278.q: Why should you not breathe in helium from balloons?
a: You do not get enough oxygen
Your voice stays high for ever
86278.e: If you breathe in helium, not enough oxygen gets into your lungs. You can faint, and that is dangerous.
86278.m: Do not breathe in helium from balloons.

86279.q: What are modern airships filled with?
86279.e: Modern airships are filled with helium. It is light and does not burn.

86280.q: Which gas is the second lightest after hydrogen?
86280.e: Hydrogen is the lightest element. Helium comes straight after it.
86280.m: Helium is the second lightest element.

86281.e: Helium has no smell and no taste.

86282.q: What colour does neon glow in a tube light?
86282.e: When electricity flows through neon, it glows reddish orange. Other colours come from other gases or coloured tubes.

86283.q: What is neon at room temperature?
86283.e: Neon is a gas. You cannot see it at room temperature.

86284.q: Where is neon gas obtained from?
86284.e: There is a tiny amount of neon in the air. It is obtained by cooling air down a lot and separating it.
86284.m: Neon is obtained from the air.

86285.q: What does the name neon mean?
86285.e: ‘Neos’ means ‘new’ in Greek. Neon was newly discovered in 1898.
86285.m: The name neon means ‘the new one’.

86286.q: Which group of substances does neon belong to?
86286.e: Neon is a noble gas, like helium and argon. Noble gases hardly combine with other substances.
86286.m: Neon is one of the noble gases.

86287.e: Neon colours are loud and glowing, for example neon yellow. They are called that because they remind people of glowing neon tubes.
86287.m: Neon colours are bright and glowing.

86288.q: What are glowing advertising signs made of gas tubes called?
86288.e: Glowing writing made of bent glass tubes is called a neon sign. You see them on shops and cinemas.
86288.m: Neon signs glow in glass tubes.

a: Yes, even just looking at it
86289.e: Neon is not poisonous. It hardly reacts with other substances.

86290.q: What does a B on a pencil mean?
86290.e: B stands for ‘black’. A B pencil contains a lot of graphite and writes soft and dark.
86290.m: A B pencil writes soft and dark.

86291.q: What can you use to lubricate a sticking door lock?
86291.e: Graphite is smooth and lubricates without being sticky. That is why fine graphite powder helps with sticking locks.
86291.m: Graphite powder makes locks turn more easily.

86292.q: Why can you rub out pencil lines?
a: The graphite only lies on top of the paper
The line is made of water
86292.e: When you write, tiny bits of graphite stay on the paper. The rubber picks them up again.
86292.m: You can rub out pencil because the graphite only sits on top.

86293.e: Graphite is greyish black and a little shiny. That is why a pencil writes grey.

86294.e: The layers in graphite slide easily over each other. That is why it feels smooth and greasy.

86295.e: Graphite conducts electricity even though it is not a metal. That is why it is used in batteries, for example.

86296.q: Why is the core of a pencil called ‘lead’?
a: People used to think graphite was lead
It is as heavy as lead
Its casing used to be made of lead
86296.e: In the past, people thought graphite was a kind of lead. The name stuck, even though there is no lead in it.
86296.m: There is no lead in a pencil.

86297.q: What does the Greek word that ‘graphite’ comes from mean?
86297.e: ‘Graphein’ means ‘to write’ in Greek. You can write with graphite.
86297.m: Graphite comes from the Greek word for ‘to write’.

86298.q: Why is chlorine added to swimming pool water?
86298.e: Chlorine kills bacteria and other germs. That keeps the pool water clean.

86299.q: When does an indoor pool smell especially strongly of ‘chlorine’?
a: When there is a lot of sweat in the water
When the water is completely clean
When the sun is shining outside
When only a few people are swimming
86299.e: The typical pool smell forms when chlorine reacts with sweat, wee and dirt. That is why you shower before swimming.
86299.m: Showering before swimming helps against the chlorine smell.

86300.e: Pure chlorine is yellowish green. Its name comes from the Greek word for ‘yellowish green’.

86301.q: Which element is found together with sodium in table salt?
86301.e: The chemical name for table salt is sodium chloride. It is made of sodium and chlorine.
86301.m: Table salt is made of sodium and chlorine.

86302.q: What protects your eyes from chlorinated water when swimming?
86302.e: Chlorinated water can irritate the eyes. Swimming goggles keep the water away from your eyes.
86302.m: Swimming goggles protect your eyes in the pool.

86303.e: Pure chlorine is very poisonous. But in a swimming pool there is only a tiny amount of chlorine in the water.

86304.q: What can chlorinated water do to colourful swimwear?
86304.e: Chlorine bleaches colours. That is why swimwear gets paler over time.

86305.q: What is chlorine at room temperature?
86305.e: Pure chlorine is a gas at room temperature. It is heavier than air.

86306.q: What is fluoride in toothpaste good for?
86306.e: Fluoride makes tooth enamel harder. That way teeth do not get holes so quickly.

86307.q: About how much toothpaste do small children need?
86307.e: For small children, an amount the size of a pea is enough. That is enough to protect the teeth.
86307.m: Small children only need a pea-sized amount of toothpaste.

86308.q: What do you do with the toothpaste foam after brushing your teeth?
86308.e: You do not swallow toothpaste. You spit out the foam.

86309.q: Which food can you also buy with fluoride in Switzerland?
86309.e: In Switzerland there is table salt with iodine and fluoride. It helps to protect teeth.
86309.m: In Switzerland there is salt with fluoride.

86310.q: Which thing that you use every day contains fluoride?
86310.e: Fluoride in toothpaste makes teeth stronger. That is why you brush them with toothpaste.

86311.q: Which drink naturally contains quite a lot of fluoride?
86311.e: Tea plants take up fluoride from the soil. That is why black tea contains quite a lot of it.

86312.q: What is pure fluorine at room temperature?
86312.e: Pure fluorine is a pale yellow gas. It is very poisonous and reacts violently.
86312.m: Pure fluorine is a poisonous gas.

86313.q: What forms as a white layer in the kettle?
86313.e: Tap water contains dissolved lime. When it boils, the lime is left behind as a white layer.
86313.m: Limescale forms white crusts in the kettle.

86314.q: Which animals build huge reefs of lime in the sea?
86314.e: Corals are tiny animals. They build skeletons of lime, and these grow into large reefs.
86314.m: Coral reefs are made of lime.

86315.q: Which rock are the Jura mountains mostly made of?
86315.e: The Jura is mostly made of limestone. It formed long ago at the bottom of a sea.
86315.m: The Jura is made of limestone.

86316.q: What are seashells and snail shells made of?
86316.e: Mussels and snails build their shells from lime. They take the lime from the water or from their food.
86316.m: Mussels build their shells from lime.

86317.q: What is the shell of a hen's egg mainly made of?
86317.e: Eggshells are almost entirely made of lime. The hen needs a lot of lime from its food for this.

86318.q: What are stalactites and stalagmites in caves made of?
86318.e: Water with dissolved lime drips from the cave ceiling. The lime is left behind and grows very slowly into stalactites and stalagmites.
86318.m: Stalactites and stalagmites grow from lime.

86319.q: What is tap water with a lot of lime in it called?
86319.e: Water with a lot of lime is called hard water. Water with little lime is called soft water.
86319.m: Water with a lot of lime is called hard.

86320.q: What happens when you drip vinegar onto a piece of limestone?
86320.e: Vinegar is an acid and reacts with lime. A gas forms, and it fizzes.
86320.m: Limestone fizzes when vinegar touches it.

86321.q: Which gas forms when lime reacts with acid?
86321.e: Lime contains carbon and oxygen. With acid, it produces the gas carbon dioxide.
86321.m: Lime and acid give carbon dioxide.

86322.e: Pure sulphur is light yellow. It is found as yellow crystals.

86323.q: What do many substances containing sulphur smell of?
86323.e: Hydrogen sulphide smells of rotten eggs. Pure sulphur itself hardly smells.
86323.m: Some sulphur substances stink of rotten eggs.

86324.q: Where is sulphur often found in nature?
86324.e: Gases containing sulphur come out of volcanoes. Yellow sulphur settles there.
86324.m: Yellow sulphur is found at volcanoes.

86325.q: What is in the head of many matches?
86325.e: The head of many matches contains sulphur. It helps the wood catch fire.

86326.q: Is pure sulphur solid, liquid or a gas at room temperature?
86326.e: Pure sulphur is a solid. It only melts at about 115 degrees.

86327.q: In which town in the canton of Aargau does warm thermal water containing sulphur bubble up?
86327.e: In Baden, warm water comes out of the ground. It contains sulphur and many other minerals.
86327.m: Baden has thermal water containing sulphur.

86328.q: What colour flame does sulphur burn with?
86328.e: Sulphur burns with a blue flame. A gas with a sharp smell forms.

86329.q: Which letter is the symbol for sulphur?
86329.e: Sulphur is called ‘sulfur’ in Latin. That is why its symbol is S.
86329.m: The symbol for sulphur is S.

86330.e: Liquid nitrogen looks like water. But it is extremely cold and evaporates at once.

86331.q: Roughly how much of the air is nitrogen?
86331.e: Around 78 out of 100 parts of the air are nitrogen. That is about three quarters.
86331.m: About three quarters of the air is nitrogen.

86332.q: About how cold is liquid nitrogen?
86332.e: Nitrogen only becomes liquid at about minus 196 degrees. So it is extremely cold.

86333.q: Why does garden fertiliser often contain nitrogen?
a: So that the soil stays dry
86333.e: Plants need nitrogen to build leaves and stems. That is why fertiliser often contains nitrogen.

86334.q: What does our body do with the nitrogen from the air when we breathe?
86334.e: Our body does not need the nitrogen from the air. We simply breathe it out again.
86334.m: We breathe the nitrogen from the air out again.

86336.q: Which gas is often put in crisp packets to keep the crisps fresh?
86336.e: Nitrogen pushes the oxygen out of the packet. That way the crisps do not go stale so quickly.

86337.q: Which letter is the symbol for nitrogen?
86337.e: Nitrogen is called ‘nitrogenium’ in Latin. That is why its symbol is N.
86337.m: The symbol for nitrogen is N.

86338.q: What happens to a flower dipped in liquid nitrogen?
a: It bursts into bloom at once
86338.e: Liquid nitrogen is so cold that the flower freezes instantly. After that it shatters like glass.
86338.m: Liquid nitrogen makes flowers rock hard.

86339.q: What happens to an iron screw placed on mercury?
86339.e: Mercury is almost twice as heavy as iron. That is why iron floats on mercury like wood on water.

86340.e: Mercury shines silver like a mirror. That is why its old name is quicksilver.

86341.q: Which measuring device often used to contain mercury?
86341.e: In the past, mercury in a clinical thermometer showed your temperature. Today other thermometers are used.
86341.m: Clinical thermometers used to contain mercury.

86342.e: Mercury and its vapour are poisonous. That is why it is replaced wherever possible today.

86343.q: What do you do if an old mercury thermometer breaks?
a: Touch nothing and fetch an adult
Pick it up with your fingers
86343.e: Mercury is poisonous, so you do not touch it. Adults must get rid of it carefully.
86343.m: Do not touch mercury from a broken thermometer.

86344.q: Which planet has the same name as the metal mercury?
86344.e: In English the metal and the planet are both called mercury. In German, however, the metal is called Quecksilber.
86344.m: The metal mercury shares its name with the planet.

86346.q: What does mercury form when you pour it onto a table?
86346.e: Mercury pulls itself together into round beads. These roll around easily.

86347.q: What does our body need calcium for?
86347.e: Calcium makes bones and teeth hard and strong. Almost all the calcium in the body is in the bones.
86347.m: Calcium makes bones and teeth strong.

86348.q: Which drink provides a lot of calcium?
86348.e: Milk contains a lot of calcium. One glass of milk already covers a good part of what you need in a day.
86348.m: Milk provides a lot of calcium.

86349.q: Which food contains a lot of calcium?
86349.e: Cheese contains a lot of calcium. Hard cheese such as Sbrinz has especially lots.
86349.m: Cheese contains a lot of calcium.

86350.e: Pure calcium is a soft, silvery metal. In nature, however, it is only found in compounds.

86351.q: Which green vegetable contains a lot of calcium?
86351.e: Broccoli and other green cabbage vegetables contain a lot of calcium. Cucumbers have only a little.

86352.q: What is the symbol for calcium?
86352.e: The symbol for calcium is Ca. C stands for carbon and Cl for chlorine.
86352.m: The symbol for calcium is Ca.

86353.q: Which vitamin helps the body take in calcium?
86353.e: Vitamin D helps calcium from food get into the bones. Our skin makes vitamin D in sunlight.
86353.m: Vitamin D helps the body take in calcium.

86354.q: What happens to bones if you do not get enough calcium?
86354.e: Without enough calcium, bones become weaker. They can then break more easily.
86354.m: Too little calcium makes bones brittle.

86355.q: Which illness used to be common in Switzerland because of a lack of iodine?
86355.e: Without enough iodine, a large swelling can form on the neck. This is called a goitre.
86355.m: Iodine in salt protects against goitre.

86356.e: The thyroid gland sits at the front of the neck. It needs iodine to make important messenger substances.

86357.q: Which country was among the first to have iodised salt in 1922?
86357.e: In 1922 Switzerland was one of the first countries to introduce iodised salt. After that, illnesses caused by a lack of iodine became much rarer.
86357.m: Switzerland has had iodised salt since 1922.

86358.q: Which food naturally contains a lot of iodine?
86358.e: There is a lot of iodine in the sea. That is why sea fish and seaweed contain a lot of it.
86358.m: Sea fish contains a lot of iodine.

86359.q: Why does Swiss soil contain little iodine?
a: Glaciers and rain washed it away
86359.e: During the Ice Age and through rain, the iodine was washed out of the soil. That is why vegetables from Switzerland contain little iodine.
86359.m: Swiss soil is poor in iodine.

86360.q: What colour is the vapour of heated iodine?
86360.e: Heated iodine forms a violet vapour. The name iodine comes from the Greek word for ‘violet coloured’.

86361.q: What was tincture of iodine used for in the past?
86361.e: Tincture of iodine kills germs. In the past it was painted onto wounds.

86362.q: What colour does a potato turn when you drip iodine solution on it?
86362.e: Iodine turns starch bluish black. Potatoes contain a lot of starch.

86363.e: Pure gold shines yellow. That is why this colour is also called ‘golden’.

86364.e: Gold hardly combines with air and water. That is why it does not rust and stays shiny for a long time.

86365.q: What is a rectangular block of pure gold called?
86365.e: Gold is often cast into bars. That makes it easy to store and weigh.
86365.m: A gold bar is a block of gold.

86366.q: In which area of Switzerland do people often pan for gold in streams?
86366.e: In the streams around the Napf you can find small flakes of gold. There are also gold panning courses there.
86366.m: You can pan for gold in the Napf area.

86367.q: What is gold beaten wafer-thin called?
86367.e: Gold is so soft that it can be beaten very thin. This gold leaf is thinner than a hair.

86368.e: The Swiss National Bank owns Switzerland's gold reserves. A large part of it is kept in Switzerland.
86368.m: The National Bank looks after Switzerland's gold.

86369.e: Gold is much heavier than most substances. That is why even a small cube of gold is surprisingly heavy.
86369.m: Gold is a very heavy metal.

86370.q: What is the well-known old Swiss gold coin called?
86370.e: The gold Vreneli was minted from 1897 to 1949. It shows a woman's head.
86370.m: The Vreneli is a Swiss gold coin.

86371.q: What is used to heat the air in a hot-air balloon?
86371.e: A burner hangs above the basket. It burns gas and blows a big flame into the envelope.
86371.m: A gas burner heats the balloon air.

86372.q: What do people stand in during a balloon flight?
86372.e: People stand in a woven basket. It is light and cushions the landing.
86372.m: In a balloon you stand in a basket.

86373.q: Which brothers built the first hot-air balloons in France?
86373.e: Joseph and Étienne Montgolfier launched the first large hot-air balloons in 1783. That is why hot-air balloons are also called montgolfières.
86373.m: The Montgolfier brothers invented the hot-air balloon.

86374.q: Which passengers were the first to fly in a balloon basket in 1783?
a: A sheep, a duck and a cockerel
86374.e: Before people flew along, the balloon was tested with animals. The sheep, the duck and the cockerel landed safe and sound.
86374.m: The first balloon passengers were animals.

86375.q: How does a balloon pilot choose the direction?
a: By finding winds at other heights
86375.e: A hot-air balloon has no steering. The pilot climbs or sinks until finding a wind that blows in the right direction.
86375.m: A balloon travels with the wind.

86376.q: In which mountain village in the canton of Vaud is there a big balloon festival every winter?
86376.e: Every January, balloonists from all over the world meet in Château-d'Oex. Then the sky is full of colourful balloons.
86376.m: Château-d'Oex is the Swiss balloon village.

86378.q: At what time of day do hot-air balloons often take off?
a: In the middle of the night
86378.e: Early in the morning the air is usually calm. At midday there are often gusty winds.
86378.m: Balloons like to take off early in the morning.

86379.q: How is a glider different from other aeroplanes?
86379.e: A glider glides through the air without an engine. It only uses the power of the air.
86379.m: A glider flies without an engine.

86380.q: What can pull a glider from the ground into the air?
86380.e: A strong winch on the ground reels in a long cable. This makes the glider climb into the sky like a kite.

86381.q: What is the powered aeroplane called that pulls a glider up into the sky?
86381.e: The tow plane pulls the glider up on a cable. At the top the pilot releases the cable.
86381.m: A tow plane pulls gliders up.

86382.q: What does a glider use to climb higher without an engine?
86382.e: When the sun warms the ground, warm air rises. The glider circles upwards in it.

86383.q: What do a glider's wings look like?
86383.e: Long, narrow wings help the glider glide well. That way it sinks only very slowly.

86384.q: Which birds circle upwards in warm air without flapping their wings?
86384.e: Storks and birds of prey let warm air carry them up. That saves energy, just like gliders.
86384.m: Storks soar upwards in warm air.

86385.q: What does a glider pilot do when there is not enough height left?
86385.e: If the pilot cannot find any more rising air, the glider has to land. If there is no airfield nearby, it lands in a meadow.
86385.m: Without rising air, a glider has to land.

86386.q: What are modern gliders mostly made of?
86386.e: Modern gliders are made of plastic with glass or carbon fibres. This is light, smooth and very strong.
86386.m: Modern gliders are made of light plastic.

86387.q: What slows down a parachute as it falls?
86387.e: The big canopy catches a lot of air. The air slows the fall, and you land gently.
86387.m: The air slows the parachute down.

86388.q: What did André-Jacques Garnerin jump out of with a parachute in Paris in 1797?
86388.e: In 1797 Garnerin went up in a balloon and then jumped with his parachute. There were no aeroplanes yet back then.
86388.m: The first parachute jumps were made from balloons.

86389.q: What is the canopy of a parachute made of?
86389.e: The canopy is made of a light, very tear-resistant fabric. That way it can be folded up small.
86389.m: A parachute is made of strong fabric.

86390.q: Which plant has seeds that fly like tiny parachutes?
86390.e: Every dandelion seed has a fine little umbrella. With it the wind carries it far away.
86390.m: Dandelion seeds fly like tiny parachutes.

86391.q: What do skydivers always carry for safety?
86391.e: If the first canopy does not open properly, there is a reserve parachute. It is also packed in the backpack.

86392.q: What do many space capsules use to slow down just before landing?
86392.e: Space capsules are very fast when they come back. Big parachutes slow them down before landing.
86392.m: Space capsules land with parachutes too.

86393.q: What is the wing called that you can take off with from a mountain and fly for a long time?
86393.e: A paraglider is a wing made of fabric. You take off from a slope and glide through the air for a long time.
86393.m: With a paraglider you fly from the mountain to the valley.

86394.q: When does a skydiver open the parachute?
86394.e: The canopy needs some time and height to open fully. That is why you open it in good time, high above the ground.
86394.m: A parachute needs enough height to open.

86395.q: What do you need to make a kite fly?
86395.e: The wind pushes against the surface of the kite. Because the string holds it, it rises upwards.

86396.q: In which country were kites invented a very long time ago?
86396.e: People in China were flying kites more than 2000 years ago. Later they came to Europe.

86397.q: What do you hold a kite by?
86397.e: The kite hangs on a long string. That way it stays in the wind and does not fly away.
86397.m: A kite hangs on a string.

86398.q: Why does a simple kite have a long tail?
86398.e: The tail keeps the kite straight. Without it, it easily spins round and crashes.
86398.m: The tail keeps the kite steady.

86399.q: What is the sport called where a kite pulls a person on a board across the water?
86399.e: In kitesurfing a large steerable kite pulls the athlete, who stands on a board.
86399.m: In kitesurfing a kite pulls you across the water.

86400.q: In which season do people here like to fly kites?
86400.e: In autumn there is often a good wind. The fields have been harvested, so there is plenty of space.

86401.q: What can you use to build a simple kite yourself?
86401.e: Two light wooden sticks form a cross. You stretch paper or thin fabric over them.
86401.m: You build a kite from sticks and paper.

86402.q: What is a kite with two strings that you can steer called?
86402.e: With two strings you can steer a stunt kite left and right. You can even fly loops.
86402.m: You steer a stunt kite with two strings.

86403.q: What do you need to make a paper aeroplane?
86403.e: For a simple paper aeroplane you only need a sheet of paper. You fold it into a plane.
86403.m: A paper aeroplane needs only a sheet of paper.

86404.q: How do you turn a sheet of paper into a paper aeroplane?
86404.e: A paper aeroplane is made by clever folding. You do not need any glue.

86405.q: Which paper is good for a paper aeroplane?
86405.e: Light, smooth paper is easy to fold and glides well. Thick cardboard is too heavy.

86406.q: What happens if you bend the back edges of the wings up a little?
86406.e: The bent-up edges push the tail down. This lifts the nose and the plane climbs.
86406.m: Bent-up edges make the plane climb.

86407.q: Why should you never aim a paper aeroplane at people?
a: The tip can hit an eye
86407.e: The pointed nose can injure an eye. That is why you only throw paper aeroplanes where there is nobody.
86407.m: Never throw paper aeroplanes at people.

86408.q: What is the Japanese art of paper folding called?
86408.e: Origami means paper folding in Japanese. Many paper aeroplanes are little works of origami too.
86408.m: Origami is the Japanese art of paper folding.

86409.q: Why does a wet paper aeroplane fly badly?
86409.e: Wet paper soaks up water and gets heavy. The wings go soft and lose their shape.

86410.q: Where does a hydrofoil have its wings?
a: Under the hull in the water
At the front of the bow in the air
86410.e: The foils sit on struts under the boat. They are always in the water.
86410.m: A hydrofoil's foils are in the water.

86411.q: What happens to the hull of a hydrofoil at high speed?
a: It rises out of the water
86411.e: At high speed the wings under the water create lift. The hull is then lifted out of the water.
86411.m: At high speed the hull floats above the water.

86412.q: Why can a hydrofoil go so fast?
a: The water slows the hull down less
86412.e: Only the small wings are still in the water. That is why the water slows it down much less.
86412.m: Less water on the hull means less braking.

86413.q: How do the underwater wings of a hydrofoil work?
86413.e: The wings lift the boat just as aeroplane wings carry a plane in the air. Only they work in water.
86413.m: Foils lift a boat like wings lift a plane.

86414.q: What can modern racing yachts with hydrofoils do?
86414.e: Some racing yachts have hydrofoils. With enough wind they lift out of the water and race over it.
86414.m: Racing boats with foils float above the water.

86415.q: Why does a fast hydrofoil rock less in waves?
a: The hull is above the waves
It has an engine at the back
86415.e: The hull floats above the waves. Only the slim struts cut through the water.
86415.m: A hydrofoil glides over the waves.

a: A boat that floats fast above the water
A boat that flies into the air
A boat that travels under water
A boat with wheels for land
86416.e: Under the boat there are small wings in the water. At high speed they lift the hull out of the water.
86416.m: A hydrofoil floats above the water at high speed.

86417.q: What happens when a hydrofoil slows down?
a: The hull sinks back into the water
86417.e: When the boat slows down, the wings no longer carry enough. Then the hull sits in the water again like an ordinary boat.
86417.m: At low speed a hydrofoil moves like an ordinary boat.

86418.e: The submarine lets water into large tanks. This makes it heavier and it sinks.
86418.m: A submarine dives by taking in water.

86419.q: How does a submarine get back to the surface?
a: It pushes the water out with air
86419.e: Compressed air pushes the water out of the tanks. The submarine gets lighter and rises.
86419.m: A submarine rises again with compressed air.

86420.q: What device do you use to look over the water from a submerged submarine?
86420.e: A periscope is a long tube with mirrors. With it you can look over the water from just below the surface.
86420.m: A submarine looks over the water with a periscope.

86423.q: Why does a submarine need very thick walls?
a: The water pushes hard at great depth
So fish cannot bite into it
86423.e: The deeper you dive, the harder the water pushes. Thin walls would be crushed.
86423.m: Deep down the water pushes very hard.

86424.q: What is the name of Captain Nemo's famous submarine?
86424.e: Captain Nemo is a character from a novel by Jules Verne. His submarine is called the Nautilus.
86424.m: Captain Nemo sails in the Nautilus.

86425.q: What do submarines use to find their way under water?
86425.e: It is dark under water. Submarines send out sound and listen for the echo, rather like bats.
86425.m: Submarines find their way with sound.

86426.q: How do people breathe in a submarine under water?
a: With the air inside the submarine
86426.e: There is air to breathe inside the submarine. Large submarines can even make fresh air themselves.
86426.m: In a submarine you breathe normal air.

86427.q: What does a sailor do when the wind gets too strong?
86427.e: In strong wind the sail is made smaller. This is called “reefing” and keeps the boat safe.
86427.m: In strong wind you make the sail smaller.

86428.q: What is the tall pole that the sail hangs from called?
86428.e: The mast sticks up high out of the boat. The sail is hoisted up it.
86428.m: The sail hangs from the mast.

86429.q: What do you steer a sailing boat with?
86429.e: The rudder at the back in the water steers the boat. You move it with a tiller or a wheel.
86429.m: You steer the boat with the rudder.

86431.q: Which Swiss sailing team won the America's Cup in 2003?
86431.e: Team Alinghi from Lake Geneva won the America's Cup in 2003. It was the first team from Europe to win this famous trophy.
86431.m: Alinghi brought the America's Cup to Switzerland.

86432.q: On which lake does the “Bol d'Or” sailing race take place every year?
86432.e: The Bol d'Or is one of the biggest sailing races on a lake in Europe. Hundreds of boats race across Lake Geneva.
86432.m: The Bol d'Or is sailed on Lake Geneva.

86433.q: What helps a large sailing boat not to capsize?
86433.e: The keel is a heavy part under the boat. It pulls the boat down and keeps it upright.
86433.m: The heavy keel keeps a sailing boat upright.

86434.q: What do you wear on a sailing boat for safety?
86434.e: A life jacket keeps you at the surface in the water. It is very important when sailing.
86434.m: Wear a life jacket when sailing.

86435.q: What is a race between sailing boats called?
86435.e: A boat race is called a regatta. The boats sail round buoys.
86435.m: A sailing race is called a regatta.

86436.e: A paddle steamer has large wheels with paddles. They turn and push the ship through the water.
86436.m: A paddle steamer moves with paddle wheels.

86437.q: Which machine turns the wheels of a paddle steamer?
86437.e: In the steam engine, hot steam pushes on pistons. This movement turns the paddle wheels.
86437.m: A steam engine drives the paddle steamer.

86438.q: What is the steam in a steamship made from?
86438.e: Water is heated strongly in the boiler. It turns into steam, which drives the engine.

86439.q: How many paddle steamers sail on Lake Lucerne today?
86439.e: Five paddle steamers sail on Lake Lucerne today (as of 2026). They were built between 1901 and 1928.
86439.m: Five paddle steamers sail on Lake Lucerne.

86440.q: On which lake does a fleet of beautiful old Belle Époque paddle steamers sail?
86440.e: The shipping company on Lake Geneva owns eight historic paddle steamers. They were built between 1904 and 1927.
86440.m: Lake Geneva has a large fleet of old paddle steamers.

86441.q: Which paddle steamer on Lake Lucerne is named after a poet?
86441.e: The steamer Schiller is named after Friedrich Schiller. He wrote the play about William Tell.
86441.m: The steamer Schiller honours the author of William Tell.

86442.q: Where are the paddle wheels on Swiss paddle steamers?
a: On the sides of the ship
86442.e: Swiss paddle steamers have a paddle wheel on each side. They are called side-wheelers.
86442.m: Swiss paddle steamers have their wheels at the side.

86443.q: What can passengers marvel at on many Swiss paddle steamers?
86443.e: On many paddle steamers you can look into the open engine room. There you can see the shiny parts of the engine at work.
86443.m: On paddle steamers you can watch the engine.

86444.q: What did Auguste Piccard use to dive deep into the sea after his balloon flights?
a: A deep-sea submersible he designed himself
86444.e: Auguste Piccard designed a craft for the deep sea, the bathyscaphe. With it he dived several thousand metres deep.
86444.m: Auguste Piccard explored both the heights and the deep sea.

86445.q: What did Auguste Piccard use in 1931 to become one of the first people to fly into the stratosphere?
86445.e: A huge gas balloon carried Piccard and his assistant to a great height. They sat in a sealed capsule.
86445.m: Auguste Piccard flew into the stratosphere in a balloon.

86446.q: Roughly how high did Auguste Piccard get on his flight in 1931?
86446.e: On his flight in 1931 he reached 15,781 metres. That is almost twice as high as Mount Everest.
86446.m: In 1931 Piccard flew almost 16 kilometres high.

86447.q: Why did Auguste Piccard sit in a sealed sphere on his high-altitude flights?
a: The air up there is too thin to breathe
So that nobody could see him
86447.e: At great heights the air is very thin and freezing cold. In the airtight sphere he had enough air to breathe.
86447.m: At great heights you need an airtight cabin.

86448.q: Which comic character did Hergé create with Auguste Piccard as his model?
86448.e: Hergé, the creator of “Tintin”, used Auguste Piccard as the model for Professor Calculus.
86448.m: Professor Calculus is based on Auguste Piccard.

86449.q: Auguste Piccard built a special boat. What for?
a: To dive deep into the sea
86449.e: Auguste Piccard built a submersible. In 1953 he used it to dive more than 3000 metres deep into the sea.
86449.m: Auguste Piccard built a submersible for the deep sea.

86450.q: What did Auguste Piccard use to fly higher than anyone before him?
86450.e: In 1931 Auguste Piccard flew almost 16 kilometres high in a balloon. He sat in an airtight sphere.
86450.m: Auguste Piccard flew very high in a balloon.

86451.q: At which Swiss university did Auguste Piccard study?
86451.e: Auguste Piccard studied mechanical engineering at ETH Zurich. Later he also taught physics there.
86451.m: Auguste Piccard studied at ETH Zurich.

86452.q: Why did Auguste Piccard sit in a sealed capsule on his high-altitude flights?
a: Because the air up there is very thin and cold
So that nobody could see him
Because it always rains up there
So that the balloon would fly faster
86452.e: More than 15 kilometres up, the air is so thin that you cannot breathe, and it is freezing cold. The airtight capsule protected Piccard.
86452.m: In the stratosphere you need a sealed capsule.

86453.q: How is Bertrand Piccard related to Auguste Piccard?
86453.e: Bertrand is the son of Jacques and the grandson of Auguste Piccard. All three were explorers and adventurers.
86453.m: Bertrand Piccard is Auguste Piccard's grandson.

86454.q: What did Bertrand Piccard become the first to do in a balloon in 1999?
86454.e: In 1999 he travelled all the way round the Earth in a balloon without landing. Nobody had ever done that before.
86454.m: Bertrand Piccard circled the Earth non-stop in a balloon.

86455.q: In which country did Bertrand Piccard's balloon land in 1999 after circling the world?
86455.e: On 21 March 1999 the balloon landed in the Egyptian desert. It had taken off in Switzerland on 1 March.
86455.m: The balloon journey round the world ended in Egypt.

86456.q: How many people travelled round the world in Bertrand Piccard's balloon in 1999?
86456.e: Bertrand Piccard travelled together with the Briton Brian Jones. The two took turns at steering and sleeping.
86456.m: In 1999 Piccard went round the world in a balloon with one partner.

86457.q: Roughly how long did the balloon journey round the world in 1999 take?
86457.e: The journey took 19 days, 21 hours and 47 minutes. That is almost three weeks.
86457.m: The balloon journey round the world took almost three weeks.

86458.q: What did Bertrand Piccard's father Jacques achieve in 1960?
a: He dived to the deepest point in the ocean
86458.e: In 1960 Jacques Piccard dived almost 11 kilometres deep in the Mariana Trench. That is the deepest point of the world's oceans.
86458.m: Jacques Piccard dived to the deepest point in the ocean.

86459.q: What did Bertrand Piccard use in 2016 to fly round the whole world without fuel?
86459.e: The aeroplane Solar Impulse 2 flew only on solar energy. Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg flew it round the world.
86459.m: Bertrand Piccard flew round the world on solar energy.

86460.q: Where did the aeroplane Solar Impulse get its energy from?
86460.e: Thousands of solar cells sat on the wings. They turned sunlight into electricity for the motors.
86460.m: Solar Impulse flew on solar energy.

86461.q: How could Solar Impulse fly at night too?
86461.e: During the day the solar cells charged large batteries. At night these batteries supplied the electricity.
86461.m: Batteries stored the solar power for the night.

86463.q: How many pilots sat in the cockpit of Solar Impulse during a flight?
86463.e: The cockpit had only one seat. That is why the pilots took turns on each stage.
86463.m: Solar Impulse always flew with just one pilot.

86464.q: Which country did the two pilots of Solar Impulse come from?
86464.e: Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg are Swiss. They took turns flying Solar Impulse round the world.
86464.m: The pilots of Solar Impulse were Swiss.

86465.q: What did the Swiss aeroplane Solar Impulse 2 use to fly round the world?
86465.e: Solar cells on the wings supplied electricity for the motors and charged batteries for the night. The round-the-world flight lasted from 2015 to 2016.
86465.m: Solar Impulse flew round the world on solar energy alone.

86466.q: Solar Impulse sometimes flew for several days without landing. How did the pilot sleep?
a: Only briefly, about 20 minutes at a time
In a bed at the back of the plane
86466.e: There was only room for one pilot in the cockpit. So he slept only briefly, about 20 minutes at a time, and then carried on flying.
86466.m: The pilot of Solar Impulse took only short naps.

86467.q: At which Swiss airfield was Solar Impulse based?
86467.e: Solar Impulse was tested at the military airfield in Payerne. Solar Impulse 2 flew there for the first time in 2014.
86467.m: Solar Impulse was tested in Payerne.

86468.q: According to a theorem credited to Thales, what is true of the two base angles of an isosceles triangle?
86468.e: In an isosceles triangle, two sides are the same length. The angles at the third side, the base angles, are then equal.
86468.m: In an isosceles triangle, the base angles are equal.

86469.q: What does Thales' theorem say about a triangle whose one side is the diameter of a circle and whose third corner lies on the circle?
86469.e: If the third corner lies on the semicircle above the diameter, the angle there is always 90 degrees. This is true for every point on the circle except the ends of the diameter.
86469.m: Every angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

86470.q: According to a theorem credited to Thales, what does every diameter do to a circle?
86470.e: A diameter goes through the centre and divides the circle into two equal halves. Thales is said to have been one of the first to state this.
86470.m: Every diameter divides a circle into two equal halves.

86471.q: Thales is said to have found the height of a pyramid in Egypt. What did he measure to do this?
86471.e: Thales measured the pyramid's shadow at the moment when his own shadow was as long as he was tall. Then the pyramid's shadow was also as long as its height.
86471.m: You can use shadows to find the height of large buildings.

86472.q: Which substance did Thales think was the origin of all things?
86472.e: Thales believed that everything came from water. With this, he was one of the first to try to explain the world without myths about gods.
86472.m: For Thales, water was the origin of all things.

86473.q: Besides being a mathematician, what is Thales often regarded as?
86473.e: Thales is often called the first philosopher of the Western world. He looked for natural explanations and backed up his statements with reasoning.
86473.m: Thales is regarded as Europe's first philosopher.

86474.q: What is the circle above a line segment called, on which every point forms a right angle with the ends of the segment?
86474.e: The Thales circle has the segment as its diameter. Every point on it forms a right angle with the two end points.
86474.m: You can construct right angles with the Thales circle.

86475.q: Which island did Pythagoras come from?
86475.e: Pythagoras was born around 570 BC on the Greek island of Samos in the Aegean Sea. That is why he is called Pythagoras of Samos.
86475.m: Pythagoras was born on the island of Samos.

86476.q: Which formula describes Pythagoras' theorem in a right-angled triangle with the shorter sides a and b and the hypotenuse c?
86476.e: The areas of the squares on the two shorter sides add up to the area of the square on the hypotenuse. So a² + b² = c².
86476.m: In a right-angled triangle, the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the hypotenuse.

86477.q: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides of 6 cm and 8 cm. How long is the hypotenuse?
86477.e: 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100. The square root of 100 is 10, so the hypotenuse measures 10 cm.
86477.m: You find the hypotenuse by taking the square root of the sum of the squares of the shorter sides.

86478.q: What are the two sides of a right-angled triangle that form the right angle called?
86478.e: The two sides at the right angle are called the legs. In Pythagoras' theorem they stand for a and b.
86478.m: The legs form the right angle.

86479.q: Which motto is credited to the followers of Pythagoras?
a: I know that I know nothing.
86479.e: The Pythagoreans believed that the whole world could be explained with numbers and ratios. “Everything flows”, on the other hand, comes from Heraclitus.
86479.m: The Pythagoreans saw numbers as the key to the world.

86480.q: Roughly when did the mathematician Pythagoras live?
86480.e: Pythagoras lived in the 6th century BC in ancient Greece, so about 2,500 years ago. His famous theorem is still learnt at school today.
86480.m: Pythagoras lived in ancient Greece about 2,500 years ago.

86481.q: Which three numbers form the smallest Pythagorean triple?
86481.e: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5². So a triangle with these side lengths is right-angled.
86481.m: The numbers 3, 4 and 5 form a Pythagorean triple.

86482.q: According to the Pythagoreans, what do you halve on a vibrating string to make it sound an octave higher?
86482.e: The Pythagoreans discovered that pleasant harmonies match simple number ratios. A string half as long sounds exactly one octave higher; the ratio is 1 to 2.
86482.m: A string half as long sounds an octave higher.

86483.q: How long is the diagonal of a rectangle with sides of 5 m and 12 m?
86483.e: The diagonal is the hypotenuse: 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169. The square root of 169 is 13.
86483.m: You can also work out diagonals with Pythagoras' theorem.

86484.q: Which country did Blaise Pascal come from?
86484.e: Blaise Pascal was born in Clermont-Ferrand in France in 1623 and died in Paris in 1662. He was a mathematician, physicist and philosopher.
86484.m: Blaise Pascal was a French scholar.

86485.q: What did Blaise Pascal build as a young man for his father, a tax official?
86485.e: Around 1642, Pascal developed a calculating machine that could add and subtract. It is called the Pascaline.
86485.m: Pascal's calculating machine is called the Pascaline.

86486.q: Blaise Pascal was a mathematician. What else was he?
86486.e: Pascal studied air pressure and wrote down thoughts about faith and being human. After his death they were published as “Pensées”, meaning “Thoughts”.
86486.m: Pascal was a mathematician, physicist and philosopher.

86487.q: What did the experiment on the Puy de Dôme mountain, which Pascal had carried out in 1648, show?
a: The air gets warmer higher up.
86487.e: Pascal's brother-in-law carried a mercury barometer up the mountain. At the top the mercury column was lower than in the valley, because less air was pressing down on it.
86487.m: The higher you climb, the lower the air pressure.

86488.q: The pascal is the unit of which physical quantity?
86488.e: Pascal studied pressure in gases and liquids. In his honour, the unit of pressure is called the pascal (Pa).

86489.q: In 1654, Pascal wrote letters to another mathematician about a game of chance. Which area of mathematics grew out of this?
86489.e: Pascal and Pierre de Fermat thought about how to share the stakes fairly in a game of chance that was stopped early. This led to the foundations of probability theory.
86489.m: Pascal and Fermat laid the foundations of probability theory.

86490.q: Around 1970, the Swiss computer scientist Niklaus Wirth named a programming language after a French mathematician. What is it called?
86490.e: Niklaus Wirth of ETH Zurich called his programming language Pascal. In this way he honoured Blaise Pascal, the inventor of the Pascaline.
